value: colour-naive workers showed a significant overall bias towards violet (bee UV-blue) over blue (bee blue) artificial flowers in unrewarded laboratory tests (chi2 = 15.8, df = 8, p = 0.044)
units: categorical (colony-level choice bias, chi-squared across 9 colonies)

source.title: The Adaptive Significance of Sensory Bias in a Foraging Context: Floral Colour Preferences in the Bumblebee Bombus terrestris

method: behavioural: unrewarded two-colour flower choice in a flight arena (120 x 100 x 35 cm), 8 violet (reflectance peak 435 nm) and 8 blue (peak 460 nm) flowers
conditions: Colonies raised in the laboratory from nest-searching queens caught around Wuerzburg, Germany, kept in darkness so workers had no prior flower-colour experience. 9 colonies, 101 bees tested (10 to 15 per colony), 1652 flower choices; each bee tested in one foraging bout after training on 16 colourless sucrose flowers, test flowers changed between bees; colony bias is the mean across its bees. The paper reports colony median violet bias of roughly 48 to 64 % and a significant difference between the two extreme colonies (Mann-Whitney U = 29.5, p = 0.012), so the preference is a population average with strong colony variation. The earlier 2001 study's correlation of violet bias with foraging rate was positive but not significant (rs = 0.82, n = 5, p = 0.089); in this study colony violet bias correlated with colony foraging rate (rs = 0.678, n = 9, p = 0.045), and worker mass correlated with neither (p = 0.574, 0.637). Preference is a choice outcome between two reflectances, not a discrimination threshold; no side-swap or position-randomisation detail was read.
quote: In this bumblebee population, we observed a significant overall bias towards choosing violet (bee UV-blue) over blue (bee blue) flowers in laboratory preference tests (χ2 = 15.8, df = 8, p = 0.044).
note: Sentence read whole in three abutting pieces. Crossref single-DOI lookup: authors Raine and Chittka, volume 2, issue 6, e556; licence CC BY 4.0 content-version unspecified, page prints 'Creative Commons Attribution License'. Not on main or any desk branch (grep of 0000556 and species+behaviour_vision).

value: females spent significantly more time in the arm with volatiles of sweet pepper plants carrying Nezara viridula eggs than in the arm with clean control-plant volatiles (P = 0.009)
units: categorical (residence time in Y-tube arm, paired choice, linear mixed model)

source.authors: Sara Van Hee, Tuğcan Alınç, Berhane T. Weldegergis, Marcel Dicke, Stefano Colazza, Ezio Peri, Hans Jacquemyn, Antonino Cusumano, Bart Lievens
source.title: Differential effects of plant-beneficial fungi on the attraction of the egg parasitoid Trissolcus basalis in response to Nezara viridula egg deposition

method: behavioural: two-choice Y-tube olfactometer, 10 min per wasp, scored as residence time per arm, 0.8 L/min charcoal-filtered air through a bottle holding one plant per arm
conditions: Females 5 to 7 days old from a laboratory colony reared on N. viridula egg masses, acclimated 1 h, each tested once. Odour sources: sweet pepper (Capsicum annuum) plants about 6 weeks old, pot and soil wrapped in foil; Co = mock-treated control, Co_O = control plant on which two gravid N. viridula females had fed and laid eggs, used within 24 h of the egg mass being found. 5 plant pairs x 10 wasps = 50 wasps per comparison; plant positions swapped after every 5 wasps; likelihood ratio tests on linear mixed models with plant pair random. The Methods do not say whether the eggs or bugs were removed before testing, so the odour may include the host eggs themselves and is not purely a plant volatile. Six pairings were run; the same Results give nulls for Co vs Co_F (feeding only, P = 0.868), Co_F vs Bb_F (P = 0.158) and Co_F vs Th_F (P = 0.440); Co_O vs Th_O was significant (P = 0.019) and Co_O vs Bb_O significant (P = 0.009) but the text is inconsistent on its direction, so those are not logged. The effect size (about 60 % more time) is in the following sentence and is not part of the value.
quote: In two-choice Y-tube olfactometer bioassays, females of T. basalis significantly preferred sweet pepper volatiles induced by N. viridula oviposition over volatiles from non-infested control plants (Co versus Co_O: P = 0.009).
note: Sentence read whole in three abutting pieces. Crossref single-DOI lookup: nine authors in the order printed, volume 19, issue 5, CC BY 4.0 vor. Family from the paper's Introduction ('Hymenoptera: Scelionidae'); OBIS lookup failed (marine database). Lab colony with a prior oviposition-induced-odour comparison; wasps' response to the odour in a choice, no threshold or non-detection measured. Not on main or any desk branch (grep of 0304220 and Trissolcus basalis).

value: more than 90 % of workers chose the Y-maze arms treated with synthetic (Z)-9-hexadecenal at 200 and 20 pg per cm
units: categorical (share of ants choosing treated arm, solvent-only control arm)

source.authors: Dong-Hwan Choe, David B. Villafuerte, Neil D. Tsutsui
source.title: Trail Pheromone of the Argentine Ant, Linepithema humile (Mayr) (Hymenoptera: Formicidae)

method: behavioural: three-arm filter-paper Y-maze, 3 ul methylene chloride treatments, 5 ants per maze, solvent-only control arms; chi-squared tests with one-sided Dunnett-type comparison to control
conditions: Colony fragments dug from nests at Berkeley, California (summer 2011), kept in boxes at 21 to 25 C. Y-maze repeated 12 or 24 times per treatment (60 or 120 ants); per-concentration n and the solvent-control result are in Table 1, which was not readable (image), so they are not logged. Same Results: (Z)-9-hexadecenal did not attract workers at 0.2 pg per cm; a mixture of the two main natural compounds (dolichodial 6.2 pg per cm plus iridomyrmecin 11.6 pg per cm) failed to attract at subthreshold levels, and adding 0.2 pg per cm (Z)-9-hexadecenal to that mixture drew 65 to 86 % of ants, which neither part did alone. (Z)-9-hexadecenal was not detected in natural trails (GC-MS limit about 0.1 ng), so the response is to a synthetic compound at high dose and says nothing about the natural trail signal. A separate trail-following assay on a Riverside colony (11 replicates, F = 37.7, P < 0.0001) is not logged. Dose-response of a pheromone component, not a detection threshold.
quote: Y-maze bioassays also indicated that high concentrations of synthetic (Z)-9-hexadecenal were effective at attracting worker ants, as more than 90% of ants chose the arms treated with 200 pg cm−1 (…) and 20 pg cm−1 (…) of (Z)-9-hexadecenal (…).
note: Sentence read whole in four abutting pieces; the two ant-equivalent parentheses and the table reference are cut and marked. Crossref single-DOI lookup: Choe, Villafuerte and Tsutsui, volume 7, issue 9; CC BY 4.0 content-version unspecified, page prints 'Creative Commons Attribution License'. Family and order from the title as printed and main's Linepithema humile rows. Not on main as sense_chemical or on any desk branch (grep of 0045016 and species).

value: diapausing adults were significantly attracted to a suspension of conspecific frass over water in a still-air two-choice olfactometer
units: categorical (choice proportions, one-sample binomial exact test against 0.5)

source.authors: Jessica Vereijssen, Rob van Tol, Michael Rostás, Chikako van Koten, Stephen Goldson
source.title: Olfactometer-measured responses of Listronotus bonariensis (Kuschel) (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) to feeding-induced grass volatiles and conspecific frass as influenced by the weevil's seasonality

method: behavioural: still-air two-choice olfactometer (a Y-tube was tried first and gave no usable results), 4 h runs beginning 4 to 6 h after scotophase, 10 starved weevils per run, dishes rotated 90 degrees between runs
conditions: Argentine stem weevils collected from New Zealand pastures and held 1 to 3 weeks; diapausing weevils collected March to May 2011 (Treatment 1) and reproductive weevils September to November 2011 (Treatment 2); weevils were not sexed. Six paired contrasts, 15 to 29 runs each for diapausing weevils and 23 runs per contrast for reproductive weevils; undecided weevils excluded. Frass in suspension (subtreatment 6): 0.01 g dry frass from the maintenance containers mixed with 500 ul water 24 h before the assay, 100 ul on filter paper against water; Table 2 gives about 65 % choosing frass (p = 0.012), a figure read from the table and not in the quoted sentence. Reproductive-season weevils (Treatment 2) showed no significant response to any contrast (p > 0.05 in all cases). Same Results for diapausing weevils: blank against blank 48 vs 52 % (p = 0.719); damaged against undamaged ryegrass p < 0.001 but the table lists 61.4 % for the undamaged arm while the text calls damaged ryegrass attractive; damaged ryegrass with 20 live weevils against undamaged p = 0.281; damaged ryegrass against damaged plus dry frass p = 0.190; damaged plus frass against undamaged plus frass significant (p < 0.001). Contrast order randomisation is not stated. Frass is an animal product, so the response is to a mixed odour from the maintenance containers, not an isolated compound.
quote: Frass in suspension (Subtreatment 6) was also significantly attractive to the diapausing weevils.
note: Sentence is short and was read whole. Reproductive null: 'This study found no significant response of reproductive L. bonariensis populations at all ... (p>0.05 in all cases)', middle of that sentence not seen, so it is stated here but not quoted. value: in spring all 7 females tested chose the Y-maze arm bearing a conspecific male's scent trail in male-only trials (7/7, P < 0.001)

source.authors: Shannon A. Richard, Isabella M. G. Bukovich, Eric A. Tillman, Sanjiv Jayamohan, John S. Humphrey, Paige E. Carrington, William E. Bruce, Bryan M. Kluever, Michael L. Avery, M. Rockwell Parker
source.title: Conspecific chemical cues facilitate mate trailing by invasive Argentine black and white tegus

method: behavioural: Y-maze with start box, base and two arms, one arm scented by a conspecific that had walked through the base and one randomly chosen arm; trial types male-only, female-only and male against female
conditions: Wild-caught invasive tegus from near Homestead, Florida (captures 2010, 2013, 2018), held at a USDA field station in Gainesville; 7 males and 7 females, spring trials for both sexes in all three trial types, fall trials for males only; trials fully randomised, scent-laying stimulus tegu chosen at random, about 60 min acclimation; unscented bias tests showed no arm preference (males P = 0.224, females P = 0.5). Same sentence: the female preferences in male-against-female and female-only trials were marginal (6/7 each, P = 0.054 for both), which the quote keeps as 'marginal'. Males showed no arm preference for male scent (5/7, P = 0.224), female scent (4/7, P = 0.5) or both (2/7 chose female, P = 0.224); the abstract says males did not preferentially follow trails from either sex but differentially investigated conspecific scent from both sexes. Stimulus is a scent trail left by a live animal on the maze floor, not a defined compound, so substrate odour and other cues the walking tegu left are not separated. Choice outcome, not a threshold.
quote: Females (n = 7 for all trial types) in spring showed a preference for male scent in the Male-only trials (7/7; P < 0.001) and marginal preferences in the Male vs. female trials (…) and Female-only trials (…).
note: Sentence read whole in three abutting pieces; the two parenthetical statistics are cut and marked. value: adults spent most time on blue cards, then green, then violet, all significantly more than on yellow/orange and white (control) cards in a six-colour wall arena

source.authors: Sandra Lisbeth Franco-Archundia, Agustín Jesús Gonzaga-Segura, Alfredo Jiménez-Pérez, Víctor Rogelio Castrejón-Gómez
source.title: Behavioral Response of Leptoglossus zonatus (Heteroptera: Coreidae) to Stimuli Based on Colors and its Aggregation Pheromone

method: behavioural: adults released in a 130 x 250 x 50 cm arena with six 28 x 21 cm coloured cards on the walls (white control, violet, blue, green, yellow, orange), 10 min per insect, number of visits and time on each card recorded
conditions: Laboratory colony founded from adults and nymphs collected on pomegranate in Morelos, Mexico, fed corn cob and green beans; 160 adults, 40 each of virgin females, mated females, virgin males and mated males, isolated 1 h beforehand; card positions randomly assigned each morning; arena cleaned with ethanol between insects. Time on colour: ANOVA, colour F = 37.21, df = 4,140, p < 0.001 (section 3.2). Sex and mating status had no significant main effect, but the sex by mating interaction was significant (p = 0.01: virgin females spent more time on colours than virgin males, mated females less than mated males), so the four classes are pooled in the quoted ranking. The cards were printed paper described by RGB values and nominal wavelengths with no measured reflectance spectra or intensity, so the colours are not intensity-matched or spectrally calibrated. Section 3.1 (adults and nymphs counted together): 86 % of insects were on blue, green or violet, and the blue versus green count difference was not significant (chi2 = 4.94, df = 5, p > 0.05); the text gives Kruskal-Wallis df = 4 and the figure legend df = 5. Fourth and fifth instar nymphs (40 each) did not differ from each other. An attraction choice among cards, not a discrimination threshold.
quote: Adults significantly spent more time on blue than green followed by violet and these were significantly different from the yellow/orange and the white (control) (Figure 3).
note: Sentence read whole in three abutting pieces. Crossref single-DOI lookup: four authors in order, volume 9, issue 3, CC BY 4.0 vor (page metadata CC BY 3.0). Family from the title as printed; order Hemiptera as on main for Leptoglossus chilensis (desk-d226, Coreidae/Hemiptera).
